clue.text: Natural flavouring put in plonk or fruit drink

indicators.note: something put in another thing ends up sitting inside it, so one word goes inside the other

blocks.note: to plonk something down is to set it down
herbs are plants used to flavour food

explanation.surface: A wine buff complains about a natural flavour being added to cheap wine or a juice.
explanation.walkthrough: Plonk looks like the cheap-wine noun, but here it is the verb, as in plonk the glass down.
explanation.definitionFit: Sherbet is the name for a sweet fizzy fruit-flavoured cordial or sorbet-style beverage.

clue.text: Workers on a Scottish island

blocks.note: the staff are the people working for an organisation
taken as written

explanation.surface: Labourers are employed on an island off Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: Staffa is a small Hebridean island famous for Fingal's Cave.
explanation.definitionFit: Staffa is an uninhabited isle in the Inner Hebrides, off the west coast of Scotland.

clue.text: Spirit captures wild gnu in swamp

indicators.note: a captor holds the captive inside, so the spirit word goes around the rest
something wild is unruly and disordered, so these letters are jumbled

blocks.note: an elf is a small sprite or spirit
taken as written, letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A spirit seizes a wild antelope in a marsh.
explanation.walkthrough: Swamp looks like a marsh noun, matching the surface, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To engulf is to overwhelm or flood over completely, as water would swamp a boat.

clue.text: Rot or blight at root of big tree

indicators.note: the root of a word is where it starts, so only its opening letter is kept

blocks.note: the opening letter
the alder is a tree of damp ground
to dash hopes is to blight them

explanation.surface: Rot or disease is attacking the roots of a large tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At' places the blight word next to the rest. The surface invites plant disease, but Rot is nonsense talk.
explanation.definitionFit: Rot and balderdash are both informal words for senseless talk or nonsense.

clue.text: In a manner of speaking it is not pollution

indicators.note: speaking points to how the words sound when spoken rather than their spelling

blocks.note: spoken as a dialect contraction of it is not

explanation.surface: Someone insists, in a roundabout way, that it is not pollution.
explanation.definitionFit: A taint is a trace of contamination or corruption spoiling something clean.

clue.text: Feature of space traveller, sported improperly

indicators.note: something done improperly is done wrongly, so the letters are put in the wrong order

blocks.note: taken as written, its seven letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone sported a feature of an astronaut in the wrong way.
explanation.walkthrough: The space traveller is not an astronaut but a planet, Jupiter: 'planet' comes from the Greek for wanderer.
explanation.definitionFit: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a giant storm, the best-known visible marking on that planet.

clue.text: Flag of retreat interrupts surrender

indicators.note: interrupting something breaks into the middle of it, so one word goes inside the other

blocks.note: to resign is to give up or surrender
a den is a private retreat

explanation.surface: A white flag signals withdrawal and breaks into a surrender.
explanation.walkthrough: DEN breaks into RESIGN: RE-DEN-SIGN. The surface suggests a flag of truce, but retreat is a hideaway.
explanation.definitionFit: The Red Ensign is the flag flown by British merchant ships, nicknamed the Red Duster.

clue.text: Dripping is swallowed without resistance

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the letter for resistance is taken out

blocks.note: drank is the past tense of drink, to swallow
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: Beef dripping is eaten with no resistance.
explanation.walkthrough: Dripping looks like the cooking fat but means wet; DRANK loses its R.
explanation.definitionFit: Dank describes something unpleasantly damp, cold and moist, like a wet cellar.

clue.text: God is present, I assume

blocks.note: to pose a question is to present it
taken as written
to don clothes is to put them on, or assume them

explanation.surface: A believer says God is here, they suppose.
explanation.walkthrough: Present and assume read as 'here' and 'suppose', but they are verbs: present a problem, assume a disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: Poseidon is the Greek sea deity, counterpart of the Roman Neptune.

clue.text: Cafes where more toast is endlessly prepared

indicators.note: something endless has no end, so the final letter is cut off
prepared means made up or worked into shape, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, before its last letter goes

explanation.surface: Cafes where extra toast is made all the time.
explanation.walkthrough: Endlessly reads as 'all the time', but it trims the last letter off the toast word.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea rooms are small restaurants serving tea, cakes and light meals.

clue.text: Backer provides a new stage, after reflection

indicators.note: a reflection in a mirror shows things back to front, so the word for stage is read backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
N is the standard abbreviation for new
a leg is one stage of a journey or race

explanation.surface: A theatre investor funds a new stage once he has thought it over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After reflection' sounds like having thought it over, but it turns only the stage word around.
explanation.definitionFit: In theatre slang an angel is a private investor who puts money into a production.

clue.text: One's in the country here

indicators.note: being in a place means sitting inside it, so the first word goes inside the country

blocks.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe
the obvious country to choose, which then has ONES put inside it

explanation.surface: Someone abroad remarks that they are in the country right here.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as a hint to the answer, as if pointing to a country on a map and saying one is in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Indonesia is a large island nation in South-East Asia, a country one might be visiting.

clue.text: People adopt English manner by the sea

indicators.note: adopting something means taking it in, so the people word takes the letter inside it

blocks.note: folks is an informal word for people
E is the abbreviation for English
a tone is a manner of speaking or acting

explanation.surface: People at a seaside resort start behaving in an English way.
explanation.walkthrough: Folkestone is a seaside town on the Kent coast in south-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition is loose: the answer is a coastal town, a place standing beside the Channel.

clue.text: Suicide achieved nothing

blocks.note: to have done something is to have achieved it
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A grim remark that a suicide attempt accomplished nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: In Virgil's Aeneid, Dido, Queen of Carthage, killed herself when Aeneas left her.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary queen is famous chiefly for taking her own life, so she can stand for a suicide.

clue.text: 'e captured a murderer and 'e suits 'imself

blocks.note: he with the h dropped
to get a criminal is to capture him
a ripper is a brutal killer, as in Jack the Ripper

explanation.surface: A Cockney tale of a man who caught a killer and does as he pleases.
explanation.walkthrough: The dropped aitches signal the 'e for E.
explanation.definitionFit: An ego-tripper is a self-centred person who acts only to gratify his own vanity.

clue.text: Leadin' newly-wed to place of reception

blocks.note: drawing means leading or pulling along; the apostrophe drops the final g, as the clue word does
a bridegroom is a man who has just married

explanation.surface: Someone leads the new husband to where the wedding reception is held.
explanation.walkthrough: The dropped g of 'Leadin'' tells you to drop it from DRAWING too; it reappears at the start of GROOM.
explanation.definitionFit: A drawing room is the formal room in a house where guests are received and entertained.

clue.text: A harvest store erected in the citadel

indicators.note: in a down answer, something erected is set upright, reading bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
the crop is what is harvested
a silo is a tower for storing grain

explanation.surface: A grain store has been built in an ancient fortress.
explanation.walkthrough: SILO read upwards gives OLIS, completing A-CROP-OLIS.
explanation.definitionFit: The Acropolis is the ancient fortified hilltop of Athens, the citadel above the city.

clue.text: Hearts removed from confectioner's fruit

indicators.note: removing something from a word takes it out, so those letters vanish

blocks.note: H is the card-game abbreviation for hearts
a confectioner's is a shop selling sweets

explanation.surface: Fruit from which the stones have been taken, at a sweet maker's.
explanation.walkthrough: Hearts looks like fruit centres, but it is H, taken out of SWEETSHOP.
explanation.definitionFit: The sweetsop, or sugar apple, is a tropical tree fruit with sweet custardy pulp.

clue.text: Fugitive is no hunter, unfortunately

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things have gone wrong, so the letters end up out of order

blocks.note: taken as written, letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An escaped prisoner is sadly no match for a pursuer.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is fleeing and hiding from the law is said to be on the run.

clue.text: Royal wedding brings a lump to the throat

blocks.note: Windsor is the family name of the British royal house
to tie the knot is to marry

explanation.surface: A royal marriage makes onlookers feel emotional.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A lump in the throat' is the emotional idiom; here the lump is literal, a bulky tie knot worn at the collar.
explanation.definitionFit: A Windsor knot is a wide, symmetrical way of tying a necktie, sitting as a bulge below the collar.

clue.text: Denunciation of one in business

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another, so the number goes within the trade word

blocks.note: trade is commerce, business
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone working in commerce is publicly condemned.
explanation.definitionFit: A tirade is a long, angry speech of criticism or condemnation.

clue.text: A balloon, to boot

blocks.note: taken as written
to balloon is to swell up, a verb here

explanation.surface: A balloon, and something extra besides.
explanation.walkthrough: Balloon looks like a noun but works as the verb meaning to swell.
explanation.definitionFit: To boot is an idiom meaning in addition or besides, the same as as well.

clue.text: Ringing display in the Three Choirs Festival

indicators.note: something on display in a place can be seen within it, so the letters lie inside these words

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: Bells are rung at the Three Choirs Festival, an annual English choral event.
explanation.walkthrough: The Three Choirs Festival rotates between Gloucester, Hereford and Worcester cathedrals.
explanation.definitionFit: A ringing sound that persists or repeats off walls is a reverberation, the sense of the noun here.

clue.text: Rejected fielders admit enjoyin' the game

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the fielders word is read backwards
admitting someone means letting them in, so the fielders take the other word inside

blocks.note: the slips are close catching fielders behind the batsman in cricket
liking means enjoying, with the g dropped just as the clue drops it

explanation.surface: Dropped cricket fielders are let into a game they are enjoying.
explanation.walkthrough: SLIPS reversed is SPILS, which holds LIKIN: SPIL-LIKIN-S. Slips is a cricket fielding position.
explanation.definitionFit: Spillikins is a children's pastime of removing sticks from a heap without disturbing the others, also called jackstraws.

clue.text: Testing ground is another place for an MP

blocks.note: first meaning: a London cricket ground where Test matches are played
second meaning: the upper chamber of Parliament, which MPs call 'another place'

explanation.surface: A proving ground offers a politician somewhere else to go.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord's is the London home of cricket. By Commons custom, MPs refer to the House of Lords as 'another place'; an MP elevated moves there.
explanation.definitionFit: One word names both the famous cricket venue and the Upper House of the British Parliament.

clue.text: One displaying detachment

blocks.note: first meaning: a single whole number or item
second meaning: a military group sent off for a task

explanation.surface: A person who shows emotional aloofness.
explanation.walkthrough: Detachment suggests aloofness, but here it is a body of troops.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit is a single quantity, and also a squad or section of an army force.

clue.text: Homicide has sovereign tucking into more rum

definitions.note: here homicide means the person who kills, not the act

indicators.note: tucking into something puts it inside, so the coin letter goes within the other word

blocks.note: rum means odd, so more rum means odder
a sovereign is a pound coin, and L is the pound abbreviation

explanation.surface: A killer has a monarch drinking more rum.
explanation.walkthrough: L goes inside STRANGER: STRANG-L-ER. A sovereign is an old British gold pound coin; rum is British for odd.
explanation.definitionFit: Homicide can name the killer as well as the killing, and a strangler is one kind of killer.

clue.text: Dog briefly enthrals a writer

indicators.note: to enthral is to hold captive, so the dog word holds the other letter inside

blocks.note: Peke is the shortened name of the Pekingese dog
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dog captivates an author for a short while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Briefly' looks like it shortens the dog, but it signals the dog's short form, PEKE, which holds A.
explanation.definitionFit: Mervyn Peake was the English novelist and illustrator who created the Gormenghast books.

clue.text: Goddess writes about gods

indicators.note: about means around, so the writing word goes around the goddess

blocks.note: to pen a letter is to write it
Ate is the Greek goddess of mischief and ruin

explanation.surface: A goddess writes about the other gods.
explanation.walkthrough: The Greek goddess of ruin is a crossword favourite because of her handy three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Penates were the Roman household deities who guarded the family storeroom.

clue.text: As ruler, becomes dreamlike

indicators.note: what becomes something else is transformed, so these letters are rearranged into a new word

blocks.note: taken as written, letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Once in charge, someone's life becomes like a dream.
explanation.definitionFit: Surreal describes the bizarre, irrational quality of images seen in sleep.
